meta.title: Penalties Sized to the Gain: PhD catch-up
meta.author: Ameer Alhashemi

slides.title: Penalties Sized to the Gain
slides.subtitle: When do random audits stop AI agents from over-using a shared resource?
slides.notes: One sentence: I test when spot-checks actually stop AI agents from taking more than their share, and whether we can predict the penalty that does it.

slides.title: The Problem

blocks.head: AI agents share limited things
blocks.text: Compute, energy, money, a fish stock. Each agent is told how much it may take.

blocks.head: Checking is expensive
blocks.text: An overseer can only spot-check a few agents each round, like a tax audit or a fishing inspection.

blocks.head: What we don't know
blocks.text: Do spot-checks stop agents taking more than their share? And how big must the penalty be?

slides.caption: Three toy worlds with six agents each. Fishery: one shared stock. Forest: over-cutting damages your two neighbours. River: two pollutants that are harmful mainly together.
slides.notes: Keep this concrete: six agents, one renewable resource, an overseer that cannot check everyone.

slides.title: Three Questions

items.head: What must follow a catch?
items.text: A fine, a memory of the offence, or nothing: which of these makes spot-checks reduce harm?

items.head: Can we predict the stopping penalty?
items.text: Economics says cheating stops once the expected fine beats the gain. Does that hold, and can we predict it in advance?

items.head: Do LLMs follow the same rule?
items.text: If four of the six agents are LLMs, do they stop where we predict, and which gain do they act on?

slides.notes: These are the three questions the paper answers.

slides.title: How One Round Works
slides.caption: Each round: agents ask for a share, a reviewer scales every request by one factor to keep the resource at half capacity, agents take their allowance or more, the resource regrows, and a few agents are spot-checked.
slides.takeaway: Harm = the resource falling below half capacity, where it regrows fastest
slides.notes: Half capacity is the maximum-sustainable-yield level from fisheries science. Same harm line in all three games.

slides.title: The Rule From Economics

stats.label: expected fine = chance of being checked × size of the fine
= 5 t expected fine per round of cheating
what a model gained per round of cheating, with no fine

blocks.head: Cheat while the gain beats the expected fine
blocks.text: This is Becker's 1968 rule. So a 30 t fine should stop an agent that gains 4.5 t per round, and a 24 t fine (4 t expected) should not.

blocks.head: But which gain?
blocks.text: The gain from one round, or the gain over the whole game once the stock is depleted? The two differ, and that turns out to matter.

slides.notes: This is the benchmark, not a new theorem. The interesting part is testing it in advance.

slides.title: Finding 1: Catching Alone Barely Helps

blocks.head: Remembering each caught lie works
blocks.text: Memory gave less harm than audits without memory in 12 of 12 settings across the three games.

blocks.head: The numbers
blocks.text: Rounds below half capacity fell from 43–99% to 0.3–3% in Fishery and from 35–66% to 3–5% in River.

blocks.head: Audits without memory
blocks.text: Correcting only the current round removed just 10–46% of the harm.

slides.caption: Share of rounds below half capacity with lying agents. Dark: no audits. Light grey: audits without memory. Green: audits with memory.
slides.notes: Programmed agents, 64 populations per setting. The point: a catch has to have a consequence.

slides.title: Finding 2: A Predictable Threshold

blocks.head: Predicted before testing
blocks.text: From runs without audits, we predicted where cheating would stop in five new settings.

blocks.head: 5 of 5 within one step
blocks.text: Every observed threshold landed within one step of the prediction, for thresholds from 0.19 to 1.20.

blocks.head: Why it matters
blocks.text: This checks our measurement method before we try it on LLMs.

slides.caption: Observed against predicted threshold. Filled: new settings predicted first. Open: audit rate or detection varied.
slides.notes: These agents are built to optimise, so this is a validation of the measurement, not a surprise.

slides.title: Finding 3: Two Shortcuts That Backfire

images.caption: Lowering everyone's allowance to absorb cheaters made cheating pay more than no audits at all (142 vs 113).
Always checking the largest report caught 25% of liars, against 100% with random checks.

slides.takeaway: Keep checks unpredictable and covering everyone
slides.notes: Both shortcuts save audits but create blind spots. Targeting where the outcome falls short of the forecast did best in Forest.

slides.title: Finding 4: LLMs Stop Where Predicted
slides.caption: Four LLMs, 520 games, 81,232 decisions. Left: how often each model took more than its allowance, by fine. Triangles: predicted stop (open) and observed stop (filled). Right: fish left for the rule-following agents.
slides.takeaway: Predicted 30 t: Nemotron stopped at 30 t, gpt-oss one step early at 24 t
slides.notes: Gemma rarely over-took and Mistral never did, so they say nothing about the threshold. A small fine made gpt-oss cheat more (55% to about 90%): a fine works like a price.

slides.title: Finding 5: They Act on One Round

blocks.head: The gain of a single round
blocks.text: The stopping fine matched what each model took per round without a fine (4.5–4.7 t).

blocks.head: Not the whole game
blocks.text: Over the whole game their over-taking gained little or lost fish (−1.05 and 0.71 t per round), yet they kept going.

blocks.head: Easier to deter than a perfect optimiser
blocks.text: A risk-neutral agent would hold out until 36 t. Both models stopped earlier, and gradually.

slides.caption: Observed against predicted stopping fine. Points on the dashed line are predicted exactly.
slides.notes: Careful wording: this shows what predicts the stopping fine, not why the models stop.

stats.label: rounds in which gpt-oss over-took, with memory and no fine
rounds below half capacity under gpt-oss
lakes collapsed with memory (5 of 10 without)

blocks.head: Reduced, not stopped
blocks.text: Memory protected the resource without any fine, but some over-taking remained. Fines above the gain stopped it and cost no efficiency (0.99 of the maximum sustainable harvest).

slides.title: Running Now (Results Soon)

rows.question: Expected fine or fine size?
rows.design: Same expected fine (2 t or 3 t) with 1 in 3, 1 in 6 or 1 in 12 checked. gpt-oss, 20 new populations.

rows.question: Does the prediction transfer?
rows.design: 10 new populations and a reworded prompt. Predicted stop frozen in advance: 30 t for both models.

rows.question: What if nothing checks at all?
rows.design: Rules that never mention checks, compared with a check that carries a 0 t fine.

rows.question: Does cheating spread to neighbours?
rows.design: Forest ring: one programmed over-cutter, five LLM foresters; neighbours' cuts hidden or visible.

slides.notes: A fifth family, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, over-took in 80% of rounds without a fine; its predicted stop (36 t) is frozen but not tested yet.

slides.title: Questions for You
questions: Is "taking more than your allowance" a fair stand-in for an AI agent misbehaving? What would be better?
If a fine works under one wording of the rules, how far would you trust it under another?
What would convince you more: more models, or more kinds of game?
Where in your own work does someone check only a sample, and what happens after a catch?
slides.notes: Open the floor. These are the points reviewers raise too.
